# zero-server Rust core: the performance-first architecture

Written 2026-09-30. Angle: a custom per-core reactor on io_uring (Linux), IOCP (Windows) and kqueue (macOS), thread-per-core with SO_REUSEPORT, in-house parsers and codecs everywhere, the smallest vetted dependency set, and a design that targets the top of the TechEmpower Rust tier.

Evidence rule. Every technical statement below is traced to one of the research files in this directory (research-techempower.md, research-runtime-io.md, research-http-and-ws.md, research-http3-and-quic.md, research-tls-and-deps.md, research-bindings-and-handlers.md, research-db-drivers.md, research-nostd-and-security.md, research-pamoja-template.md, salvage-map.md), each of which records the URL or the local measurement behind its claims, or it is marked "unverified". Effort figures and relative throughput estimates are judgment and are labeled as such. Round 23 numbers come from the local file round23-ph.json processed by tfb-extract2.js (research-techempower.md section 3).

## 1. Goals and the yardstick

Owner priorities, in order: faster than Drogon on TechEmpower-style workloads; fully non-blocking I/O; low CPU and memory per connection; maximum security; no_std wherever the code needs no operating system; one Rust core with idiomatic TypeScript, Python and C# bindings shaped like pamoja.

What "faster than Drogon" means here (research-techempower.md sections 1, 3.11 and 7): the FrameworkBenchmarks repository is archived (last push 2026-03-24) and Round 23 is the final round, so the claim can only be established by a self-run of the archived toolset at commit 523534bb with the unmodified Round 23 Drogon entry (Drogon commit 96919df4, threads_num 0, is_fast true, connection_number 1, SyncPlugin), three machines, at least 40 GbE between client and server, five interleaved runs, medians compared, a win required in every run, ratios published beside absolute numbers, zero errors, Realistic classification. Within-run noise for identical code is 0.06 to 1.9 percent; run-to-run variance is unverified.

Targets adopted from research-techempower.md section 7.2 (Round 23 reference values):

| Test | Drogon Round 23 | Minimum win | Top-tier goal | Top-tier reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| plaintext (pipelined) | 14,655,006 (11.69M at 16,384 conns) | ratio >= 1.10 at every level, zero errors | >= 27.5M and >= 22M at 16,384 | faf 28.03M, libreactor 28.03M, may-minihttp 27.91M |
| json | 2,474,350 | >= 2.72M | >= 3.0M | libreactor-server 3.12M, may-minihttp 3.10M |
| db | 1,033,970 (drogon-core) | >= 1.14M | >= 1.30M | may-minihttp 1.36M, ntex-db-compio 1.33M |
| query q=1 | 999,446 (drogon-core) | >= 1.10M | >= 1.30M | may-minihttp 1.44M, ntex-db 1.38M |
| query q=20 | 65,211 (drogon-core), 59,192 (drogon) | >= 81.5K | >= 88K | ntex-db 88.6K, may-minihttp 88.1K |
| fortunes | 1,042,653 (drogon-core) | >= 1.15M | >= 1.25M | may-minihttp 1.33M, h2o 1.23M |
| updates q=1 | 454,275 | >= 500K | >= 520K | ntex-db-compio 478K, may-minihttp 475K |
| updates q=20 | 39,419 (drogon-core), 24,034 (drogon) | >= 55K | >= 58K | may-minihttp 58.5K, ntex-db 58.1K |
| cached queries | no Drogon entry | not applicable | >= 2.5M at 1, >= 1.0M at 100 | h2o 2.85M / 1.06M, salvo-lru 2.39M / 1.41M |

Two facts frame every design choice below. First, plaintext is a link ceiling, not a race: 28.0M pipelined requests per second times about 174 request bytes is 39 Gbit/s on the Round 23 40 GbE link, and eleven entries from five languages cluster there (research-techempower.md 3.10). Second, on the same framework and the same machine, io_uring versus epoll moves throughput by no more than 5 percent either way (ntex tokio versus compio, research-runtime-io.md 3.1), and may-minihttp leads three tests on plain epoll. The custom reactor is therefore justified by CPU per request and memory per connection, which no TechEmpower test measures, and by owning the I/O contract on all three operating systems; the benchmark wins come from the HTTP layer, the JSON writer, the allocator discipline and the database pipeline.

## 2. Crate layout

Repository shaped exactly like pamoja (research-pamoja-template.md sections 1, 2, 7 to 12): Cargo workspace with resolver 2, `crates/` holding one crate per capability plus an unpublished `xtask` and an unpublished examples crate, `bindings/node`, `bindings/python`, `bindings/dotnet` excluded from the workspace, `conformance/vectors.json` generated by the examples crate and asserted by all three bindings, `deny.toml`, `justfile`, Docker-run rustfmt and clippy, and the release workflows for crates.io, npm, PyPI and NuGet copied with renames.

Naming. The crates.io name `zero` is taken (Nick Cameron's parsing crate, 2.8M downloads), while `zero-server`, `zero-core`, `zero-ffi`, `zero-server-core`, `zero-server-http` and `zero-server-ffi` all returned 404 on 2026-09-30 (research-pamoja-template.md sections 2 and 16). The owner asked for the `zero-` prefix, so the bundle crate is `zero-server` (matching the npm scope `@zero-server`) and every member is `zero-<capability>`; `CRATE_PREFIX` in xtask `version.rs` becomes `"zero-"`. Availability of the individual `zero-<capability>` names below is unverified; any collision is resolved by suffixing `-server` for that crate only. The cdylib basename follows the observed hyphen-to-underscore rule, so `zero-ffi` yields `zero_ffi.dll`, `libzero_ffi.so`, `libzero_ffi.dylib` and `Library = "zero_ffi"` in the .NET `NativeMethods` (observed from pamoja's output, not fetched from cargo docs).

Legend: N = `#![no_std]` plus `alloc`, proven by the bare-metal CI job; S = std; A = audited crate allowed `unsafe_code = "deny"` with per-item allows and `// SAFETY:` comments; F = in the first release.

## 3. Runtime model

### 3.1 Contract

One reactor and one single-threaded executor per logical CPU, pinned with affinity; no work stealing; tasks are `!Send`; completion semantics are the internal contract on every platform (a readiness backend performs the operation on readiness and reports it as a completion, which is what compio's polling driver does); owned buffers across every await; cross-core traffic only through explicit wakes; a connection lives on the core that accepted it for its whole lifetime. This is the shape every Round 23 Rust leader uses (worker per logical CPU with affinity: xitca-web-unrealistic, ntex, salvo; research-techempower.md 4.9), and the shape monoio, glommio and compio share (research-runtime-io.md 2.4 to 2.7). Rejected: tokio multi-thread (Send bound and stealing cost; no Round 23 Rust leader runs it), glommio (Linux only), may (a stack per connection, TLS undefined across yields, guard-page segfault on overflow, one author), SQPOLL and IOPOLL (idle CPU by design).

### 3.2 The Driver trait

`zero-reactor` exposes one trait that the HTTP layer is generic over, so the h1 hot loop is monomorphized per backend and carries no dynamic dispatch:

- `submit(op) -> Token` for accept, recv, send, sendv, recvmsg batch, sendmsg batch, splice or file send, open, read, fsync, close, connect, timeout, cancel, wake; operations carry owned buffers or pool references.
- `poll(deadline) -> completions` draining a batch per call.
- `cancel(token)`, `cancel_all(fd)`.
- `wake(core)` for cross-core messages.
- `buffers()` giving a per-core pool and, where supported, a kernel-visible buffer ring.
- `datagrams()` giving the batch UDP interface (segments in, coalesced buffers with per-datagram ECN, destination and stride out), present from the first release even though QUIC lands later (research-runtime-io.md section 6, research-http3-and-quic.md 3.4).

### 3.3 Linux

Backend `uring` (research-runtime-io.md 1.1 and 2b). Ring created with SINGLE_ISSUER (6.0), DEFER_TASKRUN (6.1) and COOP_TASKRUN (5.19), the ring fd registered (IORING_REGISTER_RING_FDS, 5.18), the listener and hot files registered (IORING_REGISTER_FILES, 5.1), one provided buffer ring per core (IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING, 5.19, power-of-two entries up to 32,768, IOU_PBUF_RING_INC on 6.12 and later), multishot accept (5.19) with direct descriptors, multishot recv over the buffer ring (6.0), plain send for responses below about 10 KB and send_zc_fixed from registered buffers above it (MSG_ZEROCOPY is only effective above about 10 KB), MULTISHOT timeouts for the wheel tick and link_timeout for per-operation deadlines, msg_ring for cross-core wakes, IORING_ASYNC_CANCEL_ALL on shutdown. FAST_POLL (5.7) is what keeps socket operations off io-wq threads. Minimum kernel for this backend is 5.19 (buffer rings and multishot accept); on 5.19 and 6.0 the taskrun flags that are missing are simply not set; on kernels older than 5.19, or when io_uring_setup returns EPERM or ENOSYS, the process falls back to `epoll`. The default Docker 25 seccomp profile removed io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter and io_uring_register from the allowlist and Google runs production servers with io_uring disabled (research-runtime-io.md 2b, security posture), so the fallback is the path most container deployments take and is tested with the same weight as the primary.

The syscall surface is declared in `zero-sys` (io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter, io_uring_register through `libc::syscall`, the mmap of the SQ, CQ and SQE arrays, and the uapi struct layouts for io_uring_params, io_uring_sqe, io_uring_cqe, io_uring_buf and io_uring_buf_ring). Whether the libc crate already exports those struct definitions is unverified; the design assumes in-house declarations from the kernel uapi header. The tokio-rs `io-uring` crate (0.7.15, prebuilt bindings, `push` is unsafe) is a dev-dependency only, used as a differential oracle: tests encode the same operation through both and compare SQE bytes.

Backend `epoll`: EPOLLET with nonblocking descriptors, the documented rule to retry until EAGAIN after an edge, eventfd for wakes, recv into pooled buffers after readiness, writev for batches, sendfile(2) for static files. This is the model faf and libreactor use to reach the 28.0M plaintext ceiling (research-techempower.md 4.8 and 3.10), so nothing in the benchmark depends on io_uring.

Listeners: one SO_REUSEPORT socket per core (Linux 3.9), optional SO_INCOMING_CPU (settable 4.4) to align RX queues with cores, TCP_NODELAY on accepted sockets, TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT and TCP_FASTOPEN as listener options, backlog 1024 as ntex and actix set it (research-techempower.md 4.4, 4.5). An optional SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_EBPF program steers TCP by hash today and is the same hook the QUIC path reuses for connection ID steering.

Static files on `uring`: read_fixed into registered buffers plus send_zc_fixed for bodies above the zero-copy threshold, plain read and send below it; IORING_OP_SPLICE through a per-core pipe pair is the alternative for very large files and its kernel version is unverified in this task.

### 3.4 Windows

One IOCP per core with NumberOfConcurrentThreads 1, one reactor thread per port that lives for the process lifetime (I/O issued by a thread is canceled when it exits), GetQueuedCompletionStatusEx to dequeue batches with the timer wheel's next expiry as the wait argument, FILE_SKIP_COMPLETION_PORT_ON_SUCCESS where WSAEnumProtocols reports XP1_IFS_HANDLES so inline-completing sends never round-trip the port, PostQueuedCompletionStatus for wakes, CancelIoEx for cancellation with the OVERLAPPED kept alive until ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED arrives, TransmitFile with TF_USE_KERNEL_APC for static files (server editions have no concurrency limit; workstation editions cap it at two, so the file path falls back to read plus WSASend there). Windows has no SO_REUSEPORT listener group and SO_REUSEADDR is documented as unsafe for servers, so there is one listener with SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE and a pool of pre-posted AcceptEx calls whose completions are distributed round-robin across the per-core ports; accepted sockets are then bound to their core's port (research-runtime-io.md 1.4, 2b). Receive buffers come from a per-core pool and stay pinned while a WSARecv is pending; the zero-byte receive technique that would avoid pinning is unverified. RIO is a later optimization for QUIC sockets only, since it has no accept or connect and Microsoft publishes no numbers for it. Winsock and kernel declarations live in `zero-sys`; whether they are hand-declared `extern "system"` items or taken from Microsoft's generated `windows-sys` crate is decided by the dependency budget in section 11 (the crate is listed there as Windows-only and vetted by its publisher; its version was not fetched in this task).

### 3.5 macOS and FreeBSD

kqueue with EV_CLEAR (edge semantics), EVFILT_READ and EVFILT_WRITE, one EVFILT_TIMER carrying the wheel's next expiry, EVFILT_USER for wakes (present in the current XNU header, which supersedes the archived man page that said timers were unsupported), kevent's single-call register-and-reap batching, sendfile(2) with sf_hdtr headers and trailers for static files. Apple's SO_REUSEPORT does not distribute TCP connections, so macOS runs one listener whose accept loop hands descriptors to per-core reactors through EVFILT_USER wakes. FreeBSD comes free with SO_REUSEPORT_LB per-core listeners (up to 256 sockets). poll(2) through in-house declarations is the last resort for platforms without kqueue (research-runtime-io.md 1.6, 2b, 7.2). macOS is a development platform in this design; it gets conformance, not tuning.

### 3.6 Buffers

Idle connections hold no receive buffer on `uring` (the kernel picks from the buffer ring only when data arrives), on `epoll` and `kqueue` (read into a pooled buffer after readiness), and on IOCP only if the zero-byte receive technique proves out; otherwise one pinned buffer per pending WSARecv. Write buffers are per-core slabs; a response is serialized into the connection's write buffer and large bodies are passed as separate iovecs rather than copied. The public API exposes owned buffers in and out and never a borrowed slice across an await (the BufResult and SharedFd contract monoio and compio document, and the io_uring -EALREADY cancel semantics require it; research-runtime-io.md 5.1). Per-core arenas hold connection state, request slots, header tables and write buffers so the benchmark paths (tiers 0 to 2 and 4 in section 7) make zero calls to the global allocator per request; a counting allocator in the test suite asserts it.

### 3.7 Timers

One hierarchical wheel per core, six levels of 64 slots, 1 ms precision, two-year range (tokio's design, research-runtime-io.md 2b). It feeds the io_uring MULTISHOT timeout, the GetQueuedCompletionStatusEx wait and the single EVFILT_TIMER. Per-connection idle and header timeouts live in the wheel rather than as linked timeouts on every recv, which would double the SQE count. 1 ms meets RFC 9002's kGranularity for QUIC pacing.

### 3.8 Executor

A single-threaded executor per core with a FIFO run queue and a local queue for tasks woken by completions, polled after each driver batch; the driver is polled when the run queue empties or after a bounded number of task polls (tokio's event_interval of 61 is the reference value). Futures are `!Send`, request state is `Rc`, and the Date block, the per-core database connection and the tier 1 cache shard are thread-local values reached without atomics.

### 3.9 Cross-core traffic

msg_ring on io_uring, eventfd on epoll, PostQueuedCompletionStatus on IOCP, EVFILT_USER on kqueue. Used for: accept handoff (Windows and macOS), shutdown signals, cache tag invalidation broadcasts, WebSocket room fan-out to connections on other cores, migrated QUIC datagrams. Never on the request path of a connection-local handler.

### 3.10 Graceful shutdown

Stop accepting (cancel multishot accept, close listeners), set the per-core cancellation flag, drain in-flight requests to a deadline, cancel remaining operations (IORING_ASYNC_CANCEL_ALL, CancelIoEx, EV_DELETE), wait for every completion before freeing buffers, then join the reactor threads. Two modes as tokio offers: wait indefinitely, or a timeout after which remaining work is leaked rather than freed under an in-flight operation (research-runtime-io.md 5.3). Windows reactor threads are never recycled.

### 3.11 Allocator

Bindings use the host process allocator; the core never sets a global allocator inside a cdylib. The standalone `zero-serve` and `zero-bench` binaries offer an `alloc-mimalloc` feature because every Round 23 leader ships mimalloc or snmalloc (research-techempower.md 7.3), and the per-core arenas in 3.6 are what keep the choice off the hot path. The feature is measured against the system allocator on the TechEmpower harness before it becomes the benchmark configuration; mimalloc is C code and lands in the allowlist for binaries only, never for the bindings' graphs.

### 3.12 What is measured before the reactor design is frozen

Bytes per idle connection at 10k, 100k and 1M connections per backend (no published figure exists for any Rust runtime); CPU per request with cgroup accounting, the HttpArena efficiency methodology, for `uring` versus `epoll` on the same binary; the 500 to 600 microsecond latency step every per-core Round 23 entry shows at 16 to 32 connections versus libreactor's 39 microseconds, with per-core listeners versus a shared listener, since its cause is unverified (research-runtime-io.md 3.1, 7.3). A `driver-compio` adapter in the unpublished `zero-bench` crate runs the same HTTP layer on compio-driver as a comparison baseline; it never enters the shipped graph.

## 4. HTTP stack

### 4.1 Protocol-neutral types and the transport seam

`zero-http-types` defines `RequestHead { method, scheme, authority, path, fields }`, `ResponseHead { status, fields }`, trailers, body chunks, an `Early` marker for 0-RTT and one error enum mapped from the h2 and h3 error spaces. RFC 9114 sections 4.1 and 4.3 make HTTP/3 requests the same shape as HTTP/2, and RFC 9110 semantics give HTTP/1.1 the same logical fields once Host folds into `:authority` (research-http3-and-quic.md section 5). Three front-end codecs produce these values; the router, handlers and response writer never learn which transport carried a request.

The std seam in `zero-http` is two traits used through generics, never `dyn`, on the h1 path: `StreamTransport { poll_accept_stream, drain(reason), peer() }` and `ByteStream { read(OwnedBuf), write(OwnedBuf), finish, reset(code), stop_sending(code) }`. Reset and stop_sending map to RST_STREAM on HTTP/2 and RESET_STREAM and STOP_SENDING on QUIC; on HTTP/1.1 they close the connection. Optional capability traits `Datagrams`, `RawStreams` and `EarlyData` are denied by default and checked by the router, so WebTransport and HTTP datagrams stay out of the common path. `drain` sends GOAWAY with the last accepted stream id on h2 and h3 and sets `Connection: close` on h1.

### 4.2 HTTP/1.1 codec

In-house `zero-http1` (research-http-and-ws.md sections 2, 7, 8). Input is a caller-owned buffer; output is a `RequestHead` of byte ranges plus a consumed count, or `Partial`, or `Reject { status, close: true }`; no allocation, a caller-owned header table with a default of 64 slots (excess is 431), no clock, no global state, so the parser is a pure function that is fuzzable and never panics (`indexing_slicing`, `arithmetic_side_effects`, `unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic` at deny). Every RFC-permitted ambiguity is rejected rather than tolerated: both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length (400, close; RFC 9112 6.1 permits rejection and Drogon does the same); any request Transfer-Encoding other than exactly `chunked`; bare CR; obs-fold; whitespace before the colon (400 per RFC 9112 5.1); CR, LF or NUL in field values; differing or overflowing Content-Length values; a missing, duplicated or invalid Host; whitespace between the start line and the first field. Limits (all configurable): request line 8,192 octets (the RFC recommends supporting at least 8,000; 414 for the target, 501 for the method), 64 headers of at most 8,192 octets each, 32 KiB head (matching the h2 `max_header_list_size` so h1 and h2 accept the same requests), chunk sizes parsed as checked u64 hex with a 16-digit cap, chunk extensions capped at 256 octets, trailers at 4 KiB, body 1 MiB by default (zero-server's own `'1mb'` default) with routes opting up, Expect: 100-continue handled after head validation.

SIMD acceleration lives in `zero-simd`: explicit `core::arch` kernels for the request-target scan, the header-value scan, the header-name scan and CRLF search, 32 bytes per AVX2 iteration, 16 per SSE4.2 or NEON, 8 per SWAR word, selected through a cached detection token (cpufeatures-style cpuid on x86, compile-time NEON on aarch64). Rust 1.86 stabilized `#[target_feature]` on safe functions, so the only unsafe call site is the dispatcher (research-http-and-ws.md 6.6, 8.2). Drogon's HttpRequestParser scans one byte at a time with `std::find` and `std::equal` (research-http-and-ws.md 6.4); the design claim is only that the parser does strictly less work per byte, and any speedup is unverified until measured. httparse stays wired in as a differential oracle and as a `parser-httparse` bring-up feature.

### 4.3 Response serialization and the write path

A compile-time status-line table for every registered code; a per-core 37-byte `Date: ...\r\n` block refreshed once per second by the wheel (Drogon's `datePos_` memcpy idea without a per-response second check; may_minihttp refreshes every 500 ms in an UnsafeCell, which this design avoids by making the block thread-local); precomputed immutable header blocks per route or static asset (`Server`, `Content-Type`, `Cache-Control`, `ETag`); allocation-free `Content-Length` formatting from a 20-byte stack buffer; one vectored write per event-loop turn with large bodies as separate iovecs; chunked coding for unknown lengths; HEAD, 204, 304 and 1xx bodies suppressed by the serializer regardless of the handler; hop-by-hop fields stripped before h2 or h3 emission. This is the technique set the leaders share: may_minihttp's fixed prefix plus itoa lengths plus cached date, ntex's static heads plus DateService, actix-server's prebuilt HEAD_JSON and HEAD_PLAIN (research-techempower.md 4.2, 4.4, 4.5, 7.3).

### 4.4 Pipelining

The read loop parses every complete head in the buffer; each request takes a sequence number in a per-connection in-order ring; handlers run concurrently only for safe methods (RFC 9112 9.3), an unsafe method waits for all earlier responses; responses that complete out of order wait in their slot and all consecutive ready slots go out in one writev; a rejection marks the connection close and discards the remaining input; unread bodies are drained to a byte budget or the connection closes (RFC 9112 9.3); in-flight heads are capped at 32 per connection, leaving excess input in the socket buffer so TCP back pressure applies (research-http-and-ws.md section 10; the leaders write one batch per pipelined burst, may_minihttp with one `nonblock_write`, ntex with a write-backpressure loop). The TechEmpower plaintext test pipelines 16 requests per burst at 256 to 16,384 connections (research-techempower.md 5), which is the case this ring is sized for.

### 4.5 HTTP/2

In-house sans-I/O `zero-h2` over `zero-hpack` (research-http-and-ws.md sections 3, 11): frames, streams (idle, open, half-closed, closed), flow control capped at 2^31-1, settings validation, CONTINUATION accumulation, GOAWAY, RFC 9218 priority parsing with `SETTINGS_NO_RFC7540_PRIORITIES` advertised, Extended CONNECT for WebSocket, prior-knowledge cleartext for gRPC, no h2c Upgrade (deprecated). HPACK: 61 static entries, entry cost name + value + 32, bounded arena dynamic table, integer limits, Huffman padding rules, never-indexed literals for Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie and route-marked fields. Denial-of-service budgets from RFC 9113 10.5 with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM, plus the h2 crate defaults as starting values: `max_concurrent_streams` 100, `max_frame_size` 16,384, `max_header_list_size` 32,768, `header_table_size` 4,096, `max_pending_accept_reset_streams` 20, `max_local_error_reset_streams` 1,024, `max_concurrent_reset_streams` 50, `reset_stream_duration` 1 s, `max_send_buffer_size` 400 KiB, and a sliding window of 200 client resets per 10 s (unmeasured starting value) against the rapid reset class (GHSA-qppj-fm5r-hxr3; research-nostd-and-security.md 12.5). h2 and hyper are dev-only interoperability peers; an `h2-crate` std feature can stand in for HTTP/2 until conformance passes. HTTP/2 is not in the first release because the yardstick is HTTP/1.1 and it is the largest attack-exposed codec.

### 4.6 WebSocket and SSE

`zero-ws` (research-http-and-ws.md section 12): handshake validated in the h1 layer (GET, Upgrade websocket, Version 13, 16-byte key, Origin hook), accept value from SHA-1 over key plus the RFC 6455 GUID through `zero-crypto` into a 28-byte stack buffer via `zero-base64::encode_slice`; frame decoder over the caller buffer with the minimal-length rule, RSV bits zero unless permessage-deflate was negotiated, control frames unfragmented and at most 125 bytes, unmasked client frames closed with 1002, no interleaved fragments, validated close codes, streaming UTF-8 validation across fragments; in-place SIMD unmask (AVX2, SSE2, NEON, SWAR) so delivery is zero-copy; default 16 MiB message cap, fragment and control-frame budgets; permessage-deflate feature-gated and off by default (RFC 7692 documents the compression-plus-TLS exploit class). The three Node audit bugs (head bytes lost after upgrade, continuation frames dropped, write after close) become conformance vectors. Rooms and pools live in `zero-http` with cross-core fan-out through 3.9.

`zero-sse` (research-http-and-ws.md section 13): encoder writes `event:`, `id:`, `retry:` and one `data:` line per LF-separated line; ids with NUL rejected at the API; over h1 one chunk per event with an immediate flush, over h2 one DATA frame per event; a `:` keep-alive comment every 15 s unless an event was sent; Last-Event-ID exposed to the handler; a client decoder for `zero-fetch`.

### 4.7 Static files

Path policy checks every segment (the Node audit found dotfile checks on the basename only), ETag and Last-Modified validators, 304, byte ranges, Cache-Control from a per-route policy, precomputed header blocks per asset, and the platform file send from section 3 (sendfile, TransmitFile, read_fixed plus send_zc_fixed). Bodies below the zero-copy threshold are served from a per-core file cache with a bounded byte budget. Compression is a policy decision per route (no gzip on the benchmark routes; TechEmpower forbids it).

### 4.8 JSON

`zero-json` holds a writer that serializes directly into the connection's write buffer through a builder API (object, key, string with escaping, integer, float, array), the same idea as yarte's `Serialize` into `BytesMut` and sonic-rs into a fixed buffer; jsoncpp's DOM construction is the cost Drogon pays on the json test (research-techempower.md 4.1, 7.3). The parser side enforces depth and size caps and rejects invalid UTF-8 and lone surrogates. No serde in the core; bindings convert host values to the builder API.

### 4.9 Router

`zero-router` (no_std): method dispatch by integer id, static segments, parameters, wildcards, 404, 405 with Allow, 501, automatic HEAD for GET and OPTIONS, percent-decoding that returns an error rather than panicking (the Node audit's URIError crash), router-level middleware and query-string mounts salvaged from zero-server's router tests (salvage-map.md 2.3, research-bindings-and-handlers.md 6.6). Routes are values (section 7) so the matcher resolves a handler descriptor, not a closure, and tier 0 routes complete inside the matcher's caller without a handler frame.

## 5. TLS

rustls 0.23.x (0.24 with `rustls-aws-lc-rs` and `rustls-ring` when released) through the unbuffered API inside `zero-tls`, driven by the reactor's owned buffers; no tokio-rustls (research-tls-and-deps.md sections 2, 3, 5). Provider: aws-lc-rs by default on the tier-one targets (rustls's default, X25519MLKEM768, FIPS option), ring as the feature for no_std, wasm and toolchain-constrained builds; the library never calls `install_default()`, it takes an `Arc<CryptoProvider>` through `builder_with_provider` or `builder_with_details` because it is loaded into Node, Python and .NET hosts. Shipped `ServerConfig`: TLS 1.3 and 1.2, provider suite defaults with AES-256-GCM first and `ignore_client_order = true` for suites, ALPN `h2` then `http/1.1` (`http/1.1` alone when HTTP/2 is off; rustls picks the server's most preferred protocol and returns `NoApplicationProtocol` on no overlap), `max_early_data_size = 0`, `send_half_rtt_data = false`, `TicketRotator` with 6 h generation and 12 h acceptance, session cache 256 entries configurable to 0, `require_ems` exposed, certificate compression off, `enable_secret_extraction` only on kTLS listeners, `logging` feature off in release. Certificates: PEM through `rustls_pki_types::pem`, `ResolvesServerCert` with an atomic `Arc<CertifiedKey>` swap and `keys_match` validation for hot reload, default identity for unknown SNI, optional mTLS through `WebPkiClientVerifier`. OCSP stapling as an in-house stapler task (AIA fetch through `zero-fetch`, thisUpdate and nextUpdate validation, refresh at half the remaining interval, last good staple on failure, refuse to start a must-staple certificate with stapling off). kTLS in house on Linux (three setsockopt calls, drain at a record boundary, cmsg handling for control records, TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate reinstallation), opt-in per listener, AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 only, `TLS_TX_ZEROCOPY_RO` only for sendfile paths, user-space fallback exercised in CI (research-tls-and-deps.md section 4). Option names mirror `lib/app.js` and `lib/fetch` (`allowHTTP1`, `minVersion`, `maxVersion`, `servername`, `ciphers`) so the Node binding keeps its shape, and the three STANDARDS.md ALPN and 0-RTT statements become unchanged conformance vectors.

## 6. HTTP/3 and QUIC

### 6.1 Split

Framing and field compression are in-house no_std codecs; the QUIC transport is adopted. `zero-h3` and `zero-qpack` ship in the first release as codec crates with conformance vectors even though the listener does not, because they are byte-in, structure-out functions sharing varints, Huffman, field validation, request and response types and limits with the h2 work (research-http3-and-quic.md 4.3, research-nostd-and-security.md 14.3, 14.6). QPACK is static-only at first (advertise `SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY` 0 and `SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS` 0, the RFC 9204 defaults, which is a complete conformant implementation with no cross-stream state; hyperium h3 ships exactly this on the wire); dynamic tables are an additive feature after the fuzz corpus has run. `SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE` is sent explicitly as 32,768.

The transport is quinn-proto with `default-features = false, features = ["rustls-aws-lc-rs"]` so the single-provider rule holds, driven by the core's own reactor (research-http3-and-quic.md 4.1; research-tls-and-deps.md 8.3). Reasons: it is sans-I/O ("performs no I/O whatsoever"), deterministic, pure Rust over rustls, has DPLPMTUD, GSO and GRO, ECN, CUBIC and BBR, ack frequency and datagrams, and compio-quic proves it runs on io_uring and IOCP without tokio; it is 27,528 lines of transport logic (measured from the 0.11.18 tarball) and every surveyed QUIC stack is six or more years old with 185 to 378 open issues and daily pushes, so an in-house transport is a multi-year audit commitment. quiche (BoringSSL through cmake, NASM on Windows) and s2n-quic (tokio-bound, s2n-tls or MinGW on Windows) are excluded because they add a second crypto library. In-house around the crate: the reactor integration (datagram batches into `Endpoint::handle` and `Connection::handle_event`, `poll_transmit` batches out, the wheel driving `poll_timeout`), the connection ID allocator encoding the core index, the eBPF steering program, the 0-RTT policy layer and qlog hooks. quinn-proto is std-only with a dozen mandatory crates including `tracing`, so it sits behind the `http3` cargo feature with its own deny.toml addendum. If the owner later wants ownership, quinn-proto's crypto and congestion traits give a bounded starting point, and s2n-quic-core is the reference no_std layout.

### 6.2 UDP path per operating system

Linux: one SO_REUSEPORT UDP socket per core; connection IDs of the form [core index | random]; a SK_REUSEPORT eBPF program reads the DCID of short-header packets and calls `bpf_sk_select_reuseport` against a REUSEPORT_SOCKARRAY, long-header packets hash by 4-tuple (the kernel selftest `test_select_reuseport_kern.c` is the template; msquic encodes a server id in bytes 1 to 4 of its CIDs in production; the QUIC-LB draft formalizes the layout); without eBPF (seccomp, old kernels) the kernel 4-tuple hash is used and a foreign-CID datagram is forwarded to the owning core over msg_ring, which only happens after migration or NAT rebinding. Receive: io_uring multishot recvmsg (6.0) over the buffer ring with UDP_GRO (5.0), IP_RECVTOS for ECN and IP_PKTINFO for the destination, so one submission drains a socket with no per-datagram syscall. Send: UDP_SEGMENT (4.18, at most 64 datagrams per call) with sendmsg_zc and IP_TOS per packet for ECN; IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE so the transport's DPLPMTUD sees real loss; IP_RECVERR for the optional ICMP MTU hint; upper bound 1,452 bytes (research-http3-and-quic.md 3.1).

Windows: WSARecvMsg and WSASendMsg are overlapped calls on the same IOCP, so no second reactor; UDP_SEND_MSG_SIZE (USO) on, UDP_RECV_MAX_COALESCED_SIZE (URO) off until quinn issue 2041 is resolved, IP_RECVECN best-effort, IP_DONTFRAGMENT and IPV6_DONTFRAG, minimum Windows 10 version 2004; per-core UDP steering on Windows is unverified, so the first release consumes a single socket's completions on one core and hands datagrams to the owning core by CID through PostQueuedCompletionStatus (research-http3-and-quic.md 3.2).

macOS: no kernel GSO or GRO and the fast batching calls are private API, so kqueue readiness plus one recvmsg per datagram with IP_RECVTOS and IP_DONTFRAG; development-grade only (research-http3-and-quic.md 3.3).

### 6.3 Policy

0-RTT off by default (`max_early_data_size` 0). When enabled per listener: streams marked `Early`, only safe methods on routes flagged `early_data`, everything else deferred until handshake completion, 425 only when an `Early-Data: 1` header arrives from an intermediary, `Early-Data` forwarded by the proxy middleware (RFC 8470). Passive migration and NAT rebinding supported from the start, no `preferred_address`, 20 s keep-alive default on QUIC listeners (middlebox UDP timeouts run 20 to 30 s per msquic's deployment guidance). Server push rejected, never implemented. Transport limits as starting values: 100 bidirectional streams, 3 unidirectional plus a reserved allowance, 1 MiB connection data, 256 KiB per stream, 30 s idle, 1,350-byte receive payload, Retry under load, a reset sliding window mirroring h2 closing with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD (research-nostd-and-security.md 14.4). Alt-Svc: `Alt-Svc: h3=":<udp-port>"; ma=86400` on every h1 and h2 response when a QUIC listener serves the same certificate (never a different host, no `persist=1`), `Alt-Svc: clear` for one `ma` period after disabling, a UDP self-probe that suppresses the header when unreachable, and the operator DNS line `HTTPS 1 . alpn="h3,h2"` in the docs and the CLI doctor output (research-http3-and-quic.md 8.2).

### 6.4 When it ships

First release: `zero-h3` and `zero-qpack` codecs with vectors and fuzz targets; the datagram batch API in `zero-net`; Alt-Svc emission behind the `http3` feature. After HTTP/2 conformance: `zero-quic`, the h3 request mapping, Extended CONNECT shared with h2. Published binaries then carry `http3` compiled in and runtime-off (`listen({ http3: false })`). Promotion to default-on requires the interop runner cases (handshake, transfer, retry, resumption, ecn, keyupdate, http3) passing against Chrome, Firefox, quic-go and ngtcp2, a CPU-per-request measurement of the QUIC path with GSO, GRO and ack frequency inside the Fastly parity band with TLS over TCP (untuned QUIC did 42 percent of TLS/TCP throughput; tuned, 1 percent faster), and NAT-rebinding tests of the steering fallback. HTTP/3 does not move any TechEmpower number (the toolset drives wrk with HTTP/1.1 requests and has no HTTP/3 test) and browsers on clean gigabit links lose up to 45.2 percent data rate versus HTTP/2 (WWW 2024), so it is a product and tail-latency feature and must never add dispatch to the h1 loop (research-http3-and-quic.md sections 6, 8).

## 7. Handler model

Five tiers, from research-bindings-and-handlers.md section 6, ordered so that everything expressible as data runs in Rust without a crossing.

- Tier 0, declarative routes: static bodies, files and directories, redirects, health and readiness probes, proxy targets, rejections (rate limit, missing or invalid JWT, CORS preflight, body too large). The bound language builds the value once; Rust owns matching, conditional requests, compression and the write path.
- Tier 1, cached handlers: a handler registered with a key spec (path, selected query keys, selected headers, JWT subject), TTL, stale-while-revalidate and invalidation tags; hits served from the per-core shard with no cross-thread lock; misses go to tier 3; `cache.invalidate(tag)` is a broadcast through 3.9.
- Tier 2, data routes: the bound language registers a parameterized SQL text or a `zero-query` AST, parameter bindings from path, query, claims or validated body fields, and a serialization shape (object, array, template); Rust holds the per-core connection, pipelines the statements and serializes straight into the write buffer. This tier carries db, query, updates and fortunes for every binding.
- Tier 3, bound-language handlers, batched: ready requests queue per core, a dispatcher hands adaptive batches (1 to 256) to the language with several batches in flight; the mechanism per language is in section 8.
- Tier 4, Rust: in-process `async fn` handlers registered with the request and response types directly, `!Send` futures on the per-core executor; this is the TechEmpower entry and the Drogon-class path. A dynamic form exposes a versioned `#[repr(C)]` vtable (`zero_plugin_abi_version`, `zero_plugin_register`) with the opaque `ZeroRequest` and `ZeroResponse` handles and accessor functions that the .NET binding already consumes, generated once by cbindgen, because the Rust ABI is not stable across compilers (that statement was not verified by a fetched source).

Request views are arena slot ids (u32 generation plus index), never per-request finalizable objects; accessors return integers and borrowed byte views by default and decode strings on demand with memoization in the arena; common header names are interned integer ids. The response builder is addressed by the same slot: `status`, `header(name_id, value)`, `body_bytes`, `body_str`, `json`, `send`. Errors thrown in a handler map to the salvaged zero-server error registry inside Rust so the error path never crosses twice. Middleware that only inspects headers or the JWT is a tier 0 rule; middleware that is code is a tier 3 handler returning next.

Body rule for all bindings: request bodies are borrowed views valid only during the handler call (napi `BufferSlice`, PyO3 `&[u8]`, .NET `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`) with an explicit `retain()` copy; response bodies are copied into Rust-owned buffers below 64 KiB and transferred by reference above it with a documented no-mutation rule (napi documents the data race on shared backing stores).

## 8. Binding model

Measured floors on the owner's Windows desktop (research-bindings-and-handlers.md section 5; ratios, not Citrine absolutes): napi-rs sync crossing 13.4 ns, `External` allocation 874 ns, one Promise per request 1.8 to 1.9 microseconds pipelined (about 520k to 546k per second), ThreadsafeFunction round trip 505 to 533 ns at 64 or more in flight, batched 256 items per crossing 124 ns per item; PyO3 attached callback 36 ns, `Python::attach` from a foreign thread 2,249 ns; .NET reverse P/Invoke 2.7 ns steady state, 12.4 microseconds once per fresh native thread, view fill 1.3 ns. The shipped pamoja shape (one TSFN round trip and one mutex per request) would deliver about 1.4 percent of Drogon in Node and 0.5 percent in Python, so the per-request thread hop is what the design removes.

- Node: one context-aware napi-rs cdylib (`napi` with `default-features = false` and the lowest `napiN` level that carries the needed types), per-isolate instance data, each isolate (main thread and every `worker_threads` worker) registers its own ThreadsafeFunctions, the dispatcher round-robins batches across isolates so JS throughput scales with worker count, env cleanup hooks unregister an isolate. One ThreadsafeFunction call per batch; JS iterates slot ids through a pooled view object; sync `respond` calls complete requests; a Promise-returning handler calls the same sync `respond` later; Rust never awaits a JS Promise. Facade: `app.get("/users/:id", query("select ... where id = $1", { params: ["path.id"], shape: "object" }))`, `files("./public")`, `cached({ ttl, key }, fn)`, plain `(req) => Response.json(...)`. The `@zero-server/sdk` 2.0.0 package becomes this facade over the native package with scoped facades per capability; the vitest subset that asserts observable HTTP behavior (about 3,400 cases after dropping implementation-detail suites) runs against it through a `test/_shim/` module map (salvage-map.md 2.3).
- Python: PyO3 with one `abi3-py310` feature for GIL builds and version-specific wheels for free-threaded 3.13t and later (abi3 is ignored there), `#[pymodule]` declared thread-safe as PyO3 0.28 and later default. Workers attach once per batch and call sync handlers directly; `async def` handlers are posted to a dedicated asyncio thread once per batch and complete by a sync call; users are told sync handlers are the fast path. Free-threaded scaling is unverified (3.13t was not installed).
- .NET: `DisableRuntimeMarshalling` assembly-wide, `AllowUnsafeBlocks`, `[LibraryImport]` with UTF-8 or byte spans (never `string` on the hot path), `[SuppressGCTransition]` only on trivial view accessors that never touch I/O, locks or callbacks (Microsoft lists GC starvation, runtime termination and data corruption as the penalties), function pointers rooted for the process lifetime, `SafeHandle` per pamoja `NativeHandle.cs`, `GCHandle` for the dispatch context, resolver registration in a module initializer (the early-binding `DllNotFoundException` was reproduced). One `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` dispatch per batch with a `#[repr(C)]` batch descriptor; sync handlers inline on persistent native workers; `ValueTask` handlers continue on the thread pool and complete through a function pointer.
- Shared: the JSDoc-derived `conformance/api-surface.json` (238 exports) is the contract every binding's generated declarations are diffed against; the 484 `@example` blocks seed the guides; `conformance/vectors.json` sections start with `http1Parser`, `router`, `jwt`, `cookies`, `rateLimit`, `qpack` and `h3Frames` (salvage-map.md 2.4, research-pamoja-template.md section 10).

Expected relative throughput versus a tier 4 Rust handler on the same hardware (judgment from the measured floors): tiers 0 to 2 in any language 0.97 to 1.00; C# tier 3 sync 0.70 to 0.90, async 0.50 to 0.80; TypeScript tier 3 sync 0.30 to 0.50 on one isolate and up to 0.80 with three or four worker isolates, async 0.20 to 0.40 per isolate; Python sync under the GIL 0.15 to 0.30; Python async through asyncio 0.05 to 0.15. The advertised number for TypeScript, Python and C# users is the tier 0 to 2 number, which is the Rust number.

## 9. Database layer

Layout proven by every top Round 23 database entry (research-db-drivers.md sections 3, 7; research-techempower.md 4.9, 7.3): one I/O driver task per core per endpoint owning one socket, one write buffer, one FIFO of in-flight requests with a bounded `max_in_flight` (xitca's knob), and one statement cache; handlers on that core enqueue encoded requests and read replies lazily; the driver writes everything queued in one syscall and reads replies in order; a small per-core pool (default 1) covers long transactions; no shared cross-thread pool, because every shared-pool entry was 5 to 20 times slower (axum-pg-pool 70,385 and salvo-pg-pool 28,163 versus 1.3M on db). The top PostgreSQL entries land within about 10 percent of each other whether they use may_postgres, xitca-postgres or tokio-postgres, so the layout matters more than the crate. Drogon's FastDbClient is also one connection per event loop, so the comparison is like for like there; its gap opens on the ORM updates path (one statement per row, 24K at q=20).

Codecs are in-house no_std crates because postgres-protocol, mysql_common and bson are std-only and drag rand, base64, hmac, sha2, md-5, stringprep, flate2, serde, serde_json, regex, uuid, ahash, indexmap or time into the graph (research-db-drivers.md 2.1, 5); one fuzz harness and one conformance-vector format serve all five and all three bindings. redis-protocol is the only candidate that builds no_std and stays the documented fallback for RESP.

- PostgreSQL: extended protocol only; one Sync per logical request so an error skips only to its own Sync and results are matched by counting ReadyForQuery; explicit BEGIN, statements and COMMIT pipelined as one unit because each Sync ends an implicit transaction; binary format code 1 everywhere with in-house decoders for the common OIDs and a text fallback; per-connection LRU statement cache keyed by (SQL, parameter OIDs), names `s{n}` from a per-connection counter, Close('S') on eviction, default 256 (judgment); misses take the one-round-trip Parse, Bind, Execute, Sync path; prepared statements for the benchmark routes at connect time, all statements of a multi-query request written before the first reply is read, single-statement batched updates through `unnest` arrays or 500 pre-generated CASE statements (may-minihttp and ntex use CASE, xitca uses unnest); protocol 3.2 negotiation; SCRAM-SHA-256 through `zero-crypto`; COPY and LISTEN/NOTIFY supported but never interleaved with pipelined requests. Per-request sync point kept (xitca-web-unrealistic's single sync point crashes on database failure) and the issue 8790 resilience gate applied: survive a database restart mid-run at no more than 5 percent throughput cost.
- MySQL and MariaDB: CLIENT_PROTOCOL_41 and CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF, binary result sets for prepared statements, per-connection LRU over COM_STMT_PREPARE ids with COM_STMT_CLOSE on eviction (default 64, judgment), optimistic in-order sends on by default for MariaDB only (MySQL server behavior under back-to-back commands is unverified) plus the MariaDB 0xFFFFFFFF prepare-and-execute fast path, caching_sha2_password full path only over TLS or a Unix socket so no RSA-OAEP is needed at first, 0xFFFFFF packet continuation, compression off.
- MongoDB: no wire pipelining; a per-core CMAP-style pool (`maxConnecting` 2, generation invalidation), OP_MSG with payload type 1 for bulk writes, `exhaustAllowed` on getMore, `moreToCome` honored, SCRAM-SHA-256 with speculative authentication in hello; first release covers standalone and replica-set primary discovery; full SDAM, retryable writes and change streams deferred.
- Redis: RESP3 via HELLO 3 with RESP2 fallback, per-core pipelined connection flushed after about 200 frames or at the end of the poll cycle (fred's `max_feed_count`), push frames routed to a subscriber channel without consuming reply slots, attributes stripped and attached, dedicated connections for blocking commands; cluster and sentinel in the second release.
- SQLite: libsqlite3-sys `bundled` (SQLite 3.53.x) with the sqlite.org hardening options (`SQLITE_MAX_ALLOCATION_SIZE` at or below 100,000,000, `SQLITE_PRINTF_PRECISION_LIMIT=100000`, `SQLITE_TRUSTED_SCHEMA=0`, `SQLITE_DBCONFIG_DEFENSIVE`, hard heap limit), `SQLITE_THREADSAFE=2` with single-owner connections enforced in Rust, `sqlite3_prepare_v3` with `SQLITE_PREPARE_PERSISTENT` behind a per-connection LRU, each connection on a dedicated thread behind an async facade over a bounded channel; the wrapper trait is engine-agnostic so a `sqlite-turso` feature can follow once turso reaches 1.0 or its COMPAT.md covers the adapter's functions (0.8.1 is one day old, about 80 C API functions unsupported, WAL only, no recursive CTEs).
- Cached queries: `zero-cache` backed tier 1 route from the start, since no Drogon, may-minihttp, xitca-web or ntex entry exists and h2o and salvo-lru are the references.
- `zero-query` and the ORM: the SQL AST with per-dialect identifier whitelisting (`^[A-Za-z_][\w.]*$`) and escaping, `$eq` wrapping and `$`-key rejection for Mongo filters, request-scoped tenant predicates (the Node audit found tenancy as a process global), audit writes on every driver, schema diff for migrations; the class-based `Model`, relations, observers, seeders, factories and scaffolding stay host-language code over these tier 2 plan builders (salvage-map.md sections 4 and 6).

## 10. no_std boundary

Rule (research-nostd-and-security.md section 3): a crate is no_std plus alloc when its inputs and outputs are byte slices, buffers or plain values and it never needs a clock, a socket, a file, a thread or an OS event queue. `#![no_std]` alone proves nothing because a dependency may still link std, so CI runs both a host `--no-default-features` build and the bare-metal cross-compile for thumbv7em-none-eabihf, thumbv6m-none-eabi and riscv32imc-unknown-none-elf that pamoja already runs.

no_std plus alloc: `zero-core`, `zero-simd` (core::arch and cpuid), `zero-http-types`, `zero-date`, `zero-http1`, `zero-hpack`, `zero-h2`, `zero-qpack`, `zero-h3`, `zero-ws` (simdutf8 built without std selects kernels at compile time), `zero-sse`, `zero-router`, `zero-uri`, `zero-qs`, `zero-cookie`, `zero-mime`, `zero-base64`, `zero-multipart`, `zero-json`, `zero-jwt` codec half, `zero-pg-proto`, `zero-mysql-proto`, `zero-bson`, `zero-mongo-proto`, `zero-resp`, `zero-query`, `zero-proto`, `zero-grpc-frame`, `zero-metrics`, `zero-trace`, `zero-sdp`, `zero-stun`, `zero-env`. Attacker-keyed fields (headers, query, cookies, multipart) are bounded `Vec` pairs with linear scan, never hashbrown's default foldhash (not HashDoS resistant). The rustls crate root is itself `#![no_std]` with `alloc`, and its unbuffered API is usable without std given a caller-supplied `TimeProvider`, but its QUIC connection types are std-only and aws-lc-rs has no no_std build, so the TLS handshake is std in production and no_std only through the ring provider as a portability guarantee.

std: `zero-sys`, `zero-reactor`, `zero-net`, `zero-http`, `zero-tls`, `zero-quic` (quinn-proto is std with no `std` feature), `zero-crypto` (provider-backed), `zero-auth`, `zero-cache`, `zero-db` and the five drivers, `zero-grpc`, `zero-observe`, `zero-webrtc`, `zero-fetch`, `zero-cli`, `zero-ffi`, the binaries. faf is the existence proof that a no_std-convertible epoll server reaches the plaintext ceiling in about 7 KB of binary, but it is nightly-only, unsafe throughout and serves plaintext only; the product's no_std guarantee stops at the codecs, the router, the date cache and the JSON writer, with the I/O layer std by decision.

## 11. Dependency policy and allowlist

Two tiers (research-tls-and-deps.md section 6): zero third-party crates in every crate that does not terminate TLS, host the QUIC transport, bind the operating system or cross a language boundary; a pinned, deny-enforced allowlist for the rest. With `[bans] allow` populated, any crate not listed is denied by construction.

| Crate | Where | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rustls 0.23.x (0.24 as rustls-aws-lc-rs and rustls-ring), rustls-webpki, rustls-pki-types, untrusted, subtle, zeroize, once_cell | `zero-tls`, `zero-crypto` | the TLS engine and its hard dependencies; audited (Cure53), fuzzed (OSS-Fuzz), advisory pipeline (RUSTSEC-2026-0285 fixed in 0.23.45); `default-features = false`, `logging` off in release |
| aws-lc-rs, aws-lc-sys (67 MB of C source, `prebuilt-nasm` on Windows CI) | default provider | rustls's default, X25519MLKEM768, FIPS option; FIPS behind a separate feature never on in bindings |
| ring | provider feature for no_std, wasm and C++-free toolchains | the only no_std provider; its "An experiment." wording is why it is not the default |
| getrandom, libc, cfg-if | transitive provider needs; libc is also the syscall home for io_uring, epoll, kqueue, kTLS, UDP_SEGMENT and UDP_GRO | no `nix`, no `socket2`, no `mio` |
| windows-sys (Windows targets only) | `zero-sys` | Microsoft-generated declarations with no runtime code; version and exact feature set unverified in this task; the alternative is hand-declared `extern "system"` items, chosen if the deny budget or the audit burden prefers it |
| cc, shlex, find-msvc-tools, cmake, dunce, fs_extra, jobserver | build scripts of the providers and of libsqlite3-sys only, under `build.allow-build-scripts` | nothing else in the workspace may have a build script; `build.executables = "deny"` |
| libsqlite3-sys (`bundled`) | `zero-sqlite` | the one C library in the memory-safe core, hardened per section 9 |
| quinn-proto (`default-features = false`, `rustls-aws-lc-rs`) and its twelve mandatory crates (bytes, lru-slab, rand, rand_pcg, rustc-hash, slab, thiserror, tinyvec, tracing, getrandom, rustls-pki-types, web-time) | `zero-quic`, behind `http3` | the QUIC transport; a separate deny.toml addendum; never on by default in bindings |
| mimalloc | `zero-serve` and `zero-bench` binaries only, feature `alloc-mimalloc` | every Round 23 leader ships it; measured before adoption |
| napi, napi-derive, napi-build and their measured transitive set (32 crates, mostly proc-macro tooling) | `bindings/node` only | `default-features = false`, lowest `napiN` |
| pyo3, pyo3-ffi, pyo3-build-config, pyo3-macros and their measured transitive set (13 crates) | `bindings/python` only | one `abi3-py3XX` feature; pyo3-stub-gen dev-only |
| cbindgen | build-only in `zero-ffi` | MPL-2.0 exception as in pamoja |
| Dev-only (excluded by `exclude-dev`): httparse, io-uring, h2, hyper, h3, h3-quinn, proptest, libfuzzer-sys, arbitrary, rcgen, tokio-postgres, redis, mongodb, criterion, compio-driver in `zero-bench` | tests, oracles, benches | differential and interoperability peers, never shipped |

Explicitly off the list with the reason: tokio, mio, polling, socket2 (the reactor is in house); serde and serde_json (the JSON writer and codecs are in house; bindings convert host values); http, bytes, itoa, httpdate, memchr, hashbrown (in-house equivalents or unnecessary; memchr and hashbrown may be reconsidered only if profiling shows a win and the hasher rule holds); cpufeatures (depends on libc; the cpuid detection is written over `core::arch`, whose availability of `__cpuid` in core is unverified and confirmed on the first build); sha1_smol, base64 (covered by `zero-crypto` and `zero-base64`); tracing, log; x509-parser, der; ktls; brotli, zlib-rs (compression in house, brotli deferred); rustls-native-certs, webpki-roots (only behind an mTLS or upstream-TLS feature, noting webpki-roots's CDLA-Permissive-2.0 license); postgres-protocol, mysql_common, bson, redis-protocol, fred, rusqlite, turso (in house or deferred).

Enforcement: `deny.toml` extending pamoja's (`exclude-dev`, `yanked = "deny"`, licenses MIT, Apache-2.0, Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC, Unicode-3.0, Zlib, which already satisfy aws-lc-sys, ring and rustls-webpki without exceptions; `multiple-versions = "deny"`, `wildcards = "deny"`, `external-default-features = "deny"`, `unknown-registry` and `unknown-git` denied, no `allow-git`), run once per manifest (workspace, `bindings/node`, `bindings/python/packages/native`); cargo-vet beside cargo-deny with the mozilla, google, bytecode-alliance, isrg, embark-studios and zcash audit sets imported, exemptions only with a review date and a named owner, trust entries only for the rustls organization with an expiration; `cargo auditable` on every shipped cdylib so cargo audit bin, trivy, grype and osv-scanner see rustls and aws-lc-sys inside the native module; `Cargo.lock` committed everywhere, `--locked` in CI, `--frozen` after `cargo fetch` for releases, a `cargo vendor --versioned-dirs --locked` tarball as a release artifact; `rust-toolchain.toml` pinned to an exact version, Docker images pinned by digest, `--remap-path-prefix` and `-ffile-prefix-map` through the cc crate's `CFLAGS`, `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` from the commit, and a CI job that builds the release cdylib twice in separate containers and fails on a SHA-256 mismatch. `cargo outdated` and `cargo audit` in the weekly job per ANSSI LIB-OUTDATED and LIB-AUDIT.

## 12. Security model

- Unsafe budget (research-nostd-and-security.md sections 4, 12.1, 12.7): `unsafe_code = "forbid"`, `missing_docs = "deny"`, `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn = "deny"` workspace-wide; the audited crates `zero-sys`, `zero-reactor`, `zero-simd`, `zero-crypto`, `zero-sqlite` and `zero-ffi` carry a copied `[lints]` table with only `unsafe_code = "deny"` changed (a package table replaces the workspace table rather than merging) and a CI diff keeps the tables aligned; every unsafe block has a `// SAFETY:` comment enforced by `clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks` and `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block` at deny; manual `Send` and `Sync` only in the audited crates with justification; `clippy::mem_forget = "deny"`; cargo-geiger produces the unsafe inventory for SECURITY.md on each release. The performance-first angle enlarges this budget relative to the research baseline: four reactor backends with raw buffer-lifetime contracts are unsafe-heavy, which is the cost of owning the driver layer and the reason `zero-reactor` gets Miri (`-Zmiri-strict-provenance -Zmiri-many-seeds=0..16` where it can run without FFI), ASan and TSan jobs and a structure-aware fuzz target over operation sequences.
- Parsers never panic: `indexing_slicing`, `unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic`, `arithmetic_side_effects` at deny in every no_std crate; `overflow-checks = true` in release so a missed checked operation panics instead of wrapping; the cost is measured on the TechEmpower harness and, if measurable, relaxed only for `zero-simd` through `[profile.release.package]`, never globally.
- Release profile: `opt-level = 3`, `lto = "fat"`, `codegen-units = 1`, `overflow-checks = true`, `panic = "unwind"` (the FFI crate catches panics with `catch_unwind` because unwinding across `extern "C"` is undefined behavior and abort would crash the host process), `strip = "symbols"`; the standalone binaries may opt into `panic = "abort"`. Windows control-flow-guard in `.cargo/config.toml` target rustflags (ANSSI DENV-CARGO-ENV forbids RUSTFLAGS overrides); Linux defaults give PIE, NX, full RELRO and stack probes, verified with readelf in CI; a nightly hardened job builds with `-Z stack-protector=all` and `-Z sanitizer=cfi` to keep function pointer types CFI-clean.
- Fuzzing: one libFuzzer target per parser entry point with checked-in seed corpora from the RFC examples, the STANDARDS.md vectors and every crash artifact; invocation `-O -a -s address -- -max_len=65536 -timeout=10 -rss_limit_mb=1024 -dict=...`; weekly `-s thread` and `--careful` passes on the audited crates; Linux CI only (Windows support in cargo-fuzz is contradicted between its README and the Fuzz Book).
- HTTP hardening: the rejection posture in 4.2, 431 for oversized fields, 414 and 501, `header_read_timeout` 30 s, `idle_keep_alive` 60 s, `body_read_idle` 60 s, `request_total_timeout` 300 s (Node's requestTimeout), `max_requests_per_connection` 1,000, `max_pipelined` 32 heads in flight (research-http-and-ws.md section 10 sizes the ring at 32; the limit table in research-nostd-and-security.md section 7 starts at 8 and the harness decides), a global connection semaphore, 8 KiB initial buffer grown only on demand, h2 and h3 budgets from 4.5 and 6.3, WebSocket control-frame and fragment budgets.
- Secrets: `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` for every MAC, token, session id, CSRF token and JWT signature through `zero-crypto::verify_mac`, no `PartialEq` on secret newtypes (grep-tested), `secrecy::SecretBox` or `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` allocated once at final size, timing tests on release artifacts only.
- TLS defaults in section 5; 0-RTT off; kTLS opt-in; the io_uring backend enabled by default where the kernel and seccomp allow it, with a documented `--io=epoll` switch and an operator note that ChromeOS, Android and Google production disable io_uring for exploit-surface reasons.
- Regression catalog: the 2026-09-27 audit's roughly 120 defects become failing-first tests in the crate that owns the behavior (identifier injection, Mongo operator injection, urlencoded prototype pollution and array caps, decompression bombs with output caps, dotfile segments, percent-decoding errors, JWT algorithm confusion, JWKS kid and alg matching, WebAuthn userVerified, TURN loops and RFC 1918 relays, protobuf 64-bit varints and presence, gRPC deadlines, WebSocket framing, fetch double write, tenancy isolation under concurrency, bounded maps with expiry), kept gitignored until fixed (salvage-map.md 2.2).
- Supply chain: cargo-deny, cargo-vet, cargo-auditable, CycloneDX SBOM plus the nightly `-Z sbom` precursor, `actions/attest` on every binary, wheel, nupkg and npm tarball with `sbom-path`, publishing through reusable workflows for SLSA Build L3, weekly `cargo audit bin` over released binaries, CodeQL per language with `build-mode: none` and the pamoja `paths-ignore` for the napi glue.
- Conformance: docs/STANDARDS.md (148 sources, 515 statements) migrates into `docs/standards.toml` so xtask renders the page and checks every URL, each statement becomes a test name or a vector, and `xtask standards --check` fails when a row has no test; RFC 9000, 9001, 9002, 9114 and 9204 rows are added for the HTTP/3 work.

Cross-cutting expectations: io_uring versus epoll changes none of these by more than 5 percent (ntex compio versus tokio; research-runtime-io.md 3.1), so the numbers hold on the `epoll` fallback; `overflow-checks = true` costs an unmeasured amount and may-minihttp and ntex ship with it off; the 500 to 600 microsecond latency step at 16 to 32 connections is expected to appear as in every per-core entry until the shared-listener measurement in 3.12 explains it; Drogon moved on after its April 2024 snapshot, so the self-run pins commit 96919df4 and separately tests current Drogon.

## 14. Risks

1. The custom reactor is four backends of unsafe buffer-lifetime code maintained in house; the Round 23 data shows it buys nothing on throughput over compio or tokio current-thread, so its return is CPU per request and idle memory, both unmeasured until 3.12 runs. Mitigation: the `Driver` trait keeps the HTTP layer independent, the `driver-compio` baseline in `zero-bench` shows any regression, and the `epoll` backend is the simplest path to the plaintext ceiling.
2. io_uring is blocked by default Docker 25 seccomp and disabled on Google production; most containers run `epoll`. The `uring` backend must never be the only tested path and its security posture must be documented for operators.
3. No official round will certify the result; hardware differs; run-to-run variance is unverified (continuous-run host unreachable) and the 10 percent margin derives from within-run noise of about 1 percent and the 5.5 percent spread of the json top ten. Plaintext and json are client- and link-bound, so a weaker load generator shrinks the gap and the ceiling must be re-established with a reference server before comparing. Every actix entry failed to start in Round 23 and Drogon failed in Round 22, so the Drogon container must pass all verifications before its numbers are used.
4. The Rust leaders' fastest builds trade safety for speed (overflow checks off, UnsafeCell date caches, no method checks or error handling in Stripped builds, single sync points that crash on database failure; only 7 of the top 20 survived a database restart in issue 8790). Holding the security posture may cost a few percent, unmeasured; updates q=1 is the test with the thinnest margin (Drogon within 5 percent of the pack).
5. In-house HTTP/2 and the in-house HTTP/1.1 parser replace fuzzed, widely deployed crates; the differential oracles (httparse, h2, hyper), the RFC vectors, the Section 10.5 budgets and the libFuzzer targets are the compensating controls, and an `h2-crate` feature covers HTTP/2 until conformance passes.
6. The unsafe budget concentrates in `zero-sys`, `zero-reactor` and `zero-simd`; a bug there is memory corruption in a network-facing process. Miri cannot cover FFI and syscalls, so sanitizer and fuzz coverage of operation sequences carry the weight. Whether libc exports the io_uring uapi structs, whether `__cpuid` is available in `core::arch`, and the windows-sys version are unverified until the first build.
7. Windows accept is structurally different (one listener, AcceptEx pool, no SO_REUSEPORT) and the zero-byte receive technique is unverified, so Windows idle memory per connection may be one pinned buffer higher than Linux; Windows QUIC steering is unverified and GRO is disabled over quinn issue 2041; macOS has no GSO or GRO.
8. Dependency policy tension: quinn-proto brings twelve mandatory crates including `tracing`, aws-lc-sys brings 67 MB of C source and NASM on Windows, ring calls itself an experiment, rustls 0.24 re-cuts the allowlist and every binding lockfile together, and two providers in one build split getrandom into 0.2 and 0.4, which `multiple-versions = "deny"` flags.
9. Node throughput on tier 3 is bounded by the single JS thread (roughly 1M to 1.5M handler executions per second per isolate on the owner's desktop before handler work); multi-isolate scaling was not measured; Python under the GIL runs one handler at a time and free-threaded scaling was not measurable; all binding measurements are Windows desktop numbers and Citrine is Linux on 56 logical CPUs.
10. MongoDB is the largest and least certain driver scope; MySQL optimistic sends are unverified against MySQL server; bundled SQLite in C contradicts the memory-safe goal and turso is pre-1.0; in-house SCRAM, caching_sha2 and SASLprep are security-sensitive and need vectors.
11. HTTP/3 doubles the transport surface on a UDP path that firewalls and container port mappings treat differently; Alt-Svc advertised while UDP is unreachable delays clients, so the self-probe and `Alt-Svc: clear` are mandatory; WebTransport is still a draft in Working Group Last Call.
12. The local toolchain cannot run rustfmt or clippy; if the Docker route is skipped, CI fails and a crate already on crates.io cannot be republished at the same version. NuGet trusted-publishing policies and PyPI's new-project cap require setup before the first tag, and the `zero-<capability>` crate names are unverified for availability.
13. Effort below is judgment; the reactor and the drivers are where estimates most often slip, and the resilience gate, the conformance migration of 515 statements and the vitest shim are easy to underweight.
